q: Physics, like any other branch of science, is based on systematic observations and precise ____.
e: Physics relies on precise measurements to ensure observations are quantitative and reliable.

q: Most experiments in Physics require the observations made to be ____ rather than qualitative.
e: Quantitative observations provide numerical data essential for scientific analysis.

q: Measurement essentially is a ____ process.
e: Measurement involves comparing an unknown quantity to a known standard.

q: A standard quantity of some kind, referred to as a ____, is first established.
e: A unit serves as the agreed-upon reference for expressing measurements.

q: ____ is something or a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time.
e: A standard is the definitive reference point for a specific physical quantity.

q: Unit is a quantity or an amount used as a ____ of measurement.
e: Units provide the consistent basis for quantifying physical properties.

q: These things are known as '____'.
e: Physical quantities are properties of phenomena or matter that can be measured.

q: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a ____.
e: Every physical quantity must have both a number and a unit to be meaningful.

q: It can be expressed as ____.
e: This formula represents a physical quantity (Q) as a numerical value (N) multiplied by a unit (u).

q: where Q is the physical quantity, N is a ____ and u is the unit.
e: The numerical part of a measurement does not carry units itself.

q: Physical quantities can be classified as the basic type and the ____ type.
e: Derived quantities are formed by combining basic physical quantities.

q: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by ____ the basic (or base) units of a system.
e: Derived units are created through multiplication or division of base units.

q: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a ____ and a unit.
e: Both a number and a unit are required to fully define a physical quantity.

q: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a ____.
e: Derived units are constructed from the base units within a specific measurement system.

q: Standard is something (or) a ____ used as a measure for length, mass and time.
e: A standard serves as the definitive reference for comparison in measurement.

q: Unit is a quantity (or) an amount used as a standard of ____.
e: Units provide the standardized scale for quantifying physical properties.

q: The density of water is ____.
e: This is a standard factual value for the density of pure water at room temperature.

q: The British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the ____ system.
e: FPS stands for Foot-Pound-Second, the foundation of the British system.

q: The metric system consists of the CGS system and the ____ system.
e: The metric system is broadly divided into CGS and MKS frameworks.

q: The CGS system is based on centimetre (cm), gram (g) and ____ (s).
e: The second is the base unit of time in both CGS and MKS systems.

q: The MKS system is based on metre (m), kilogram (kg) and second (____).
e: The symbol 's' represents the second, the base unit of time.

q: The SI unit is just the modified form of the ____ system of units.
e: The SI system evolved directly from the Metre-Kilogram-Second system.

q: In ____, the Eleventh General Conference of Weights and Measures in France recommended an International System of Units based on the metric system of units.
e: The SI system was officially recommended and adopted in the year 1960.

q: This recommendation was accepted as SI units (full name, '____').
e: This is the French origin of the acronym 'SI'.

q: The SI unit has ____ base units and all other units are derived from these base units.
e: There are exactly seven fundamental base units in the SI system.

q: Sometimes a physical quantity is too big (or) too small to be conveniently expressed in ____.
e: Prefixes are introduced to handle extremely large or small values efficiently.

q: ____ are multiples or sub-multiples of 10.
e: SI prefixes scale units by powers of ten for convenience.

q: Scientific notation (or) standard form may be written as follows: Place the decimal point after the first ____.
e: This is the first step in converting a number to proper scientific notation.

q: Then determine the ____ by counting the number of places we have moved the original decimal point to the marked decimal point.
e: The exponent in scientific notation reflects the decimal shift.

q: If we moved the point to the left, then power is ____ and if we moved it to the right, it is negative.
e: Moving the decimal left indicates a number greater than 1, requiring a positive exponent.

q: The standard of length is ____.
e: The metre is the fundamental SI unit for measuring length.

q: The metre was originally defined as the length between two marks on a ____ at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris.
e: This physical artifact served as the original international prototype of the metre.

q: Nowadays the standard of length used is based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a ____.
e: This atomic standard provided a more reproducible definition of the metre.

q: A metre is now defined as the length equivalent to ____ times the wavelength of this orange-red light.
e: This specific number of wavelengths was defined to equal exactly one metre.

q: As a result, in ____ the metre was given a new operational definition.
e: The definition was updated in 1983 to be based on the speed of light.

q: The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of ____ of a second.
e: This definition ties the metre directly to the fixed speed of light in a vacuum.

q: In the CGS system the unit of length is the ____ (cm).
e: The centimetre is the base unit of length in the Centimetre-Gram-Second system.

q: In the FPS system the unit of length is the ____ (ft).
e: The foot is the base unit of length in the Foot-Pound-Second system.

q: The unit of length used by particle physicists is the '____' or 'femtometre' (fm).
e: The Fermi is a convenient unit for measuring subatomic distances.

q: In the field of optics, physicists use the unit ____, where $1\text{ \AA} = 10^{-10}\text{ m}$.
e: The angstrom is commonly used to express atomic and molecular scales.

q: In astronomy, the most suitable units are the ____ (AU) and the light year unit (ly).
e: The AU is used for distances within the solar system.

q: The light year is the distance which light travels in ____.
e: A light year is a measure of distance, not time, based on the speed of light over a year.

q: The largest unit of length is the '____' (pc).
e: The parsec is used for measuring large astronomical distances.

q: The standard of mass is a cylinder of 1 kg mass made of ____.
e: This durable alloy was chosen for the international prototype kilogram.

q: The SI base unit of time is the ____.
e: The second is the fundamental unit of time in the SI system.

q: The second was originally defined as ____ of a day, one day being the time it takes the Earth to rotate once.
e: This fraction represents one second out of the total seconds in a 24-hour day.

q: So, for accuracy, the second is now defined in terms of something that never changes: the frequency of oscillation which can occur from a ____.
e: Atomic clocks use the consistent oscillation of cesium atoms to define the second.

q: A particular frequency ____ emitted or absorbed by a cesium atom is used to define 1 s.
e: This exact frequency of radiation corresponds to the transition between two energy levels of a cesium-133 atom.

q: To measure the length of objects some ____ have to be used.
e: Standardized tools are required to ensure consistent and comparable length measurements.

q: For everyday use, the standard may be a yard stick, ruler, ____ and so on.
e: These are common, accessible tools for general length measurement.

q: Lengths are usually measured in metre, centimetre or ____.
e: These are the most common metric units for everyday length measurements.

q: Greater lengths are measured in ____.
e: Kilometres are used for measuring long distances, such as between cities.

q: In length measurement, we must choose an instrument that is ____ for the length to be measured.
e: The choice of instrument depends on the size of the object and the required precision.

q: For measuring several metres (m), the suitable instrument is a measuring tape with an accuracy of ____.
e: Measuring tapes are designed for longer lengths with moderate precision.

q: For measuring between 1 cm and 10 cm, the suitable instrument is ____.
e: Vernier calipers provide higher accuracy for small to medium-sized objects.

q: For measuring less than 2 cm, the suitable instrument is a Screw gauge (____).
e: A micrometer screw gauge offers the highest precision for very small lengths.

q: The accuracy of a Screw gauge (Micrometer) is ____.
e: This high accuracy makes it ideal for measuring thin wires or sheets.

q: The mass of an object is a measure of the ____ in it.
e: Mass quantifies the total matter contained within an object, independent of gravity.

q: Mass is measured in laboratories using a sliding mass balance or the ____.
e: These are the two primary types of balances used for measuring mass in a lab setting.

q: The electronic balance is easier to use and also ____ than sliding mass balance.
e: Electronic balances provide direct digital readings with higher precision.

q: The unknown mass is placed on the top of the pan and its mass is read directly from a ____.
e: The digital display shows the measured mass value instantly.

q: The balance really detects the gravitational pull on the object (____), but the scale is marked to show the mass.
e: Balances measure weight but are calibrated to display the equivalent mass.

q: The mass of purified drinking water of 1 litre bottle is ____.
e: This is a standard reference point linking volume and mass for water.

q: Time is measured in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, but the SI unit for time is the ____.
e: The second is the fundamental SI base unit for measuring time.

q: Most common modern clocks and watches depend on the vibration of ____ to keep time accurately.
e: Quartz crystals vibrate at a highly stable frequency when an electric current is applied.

q: The energy to keep these crystals vibrating comes from a ____.
e: A battery provides the necessary electrical energy for the quartz oscillator.

q: A stopwatch (or) a stop clock can be chosen to measure the time to an accuracy of a ____.
e: Analog stopwatches typically offer precision to the nearest tenth of a second.

q: Digital stopwatches can measure up to ____.
e: Digital stopwatches provide higher resolution, measuring down to one hundredth of a second.
